clue.text: George’s scheme involving one chasing car

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in, so one piece is wrapped around another
a chaser runs behind its quarry, so this piece is placed after the other

blocks.note: an automatic is a car with self-changing gears
a plot is a scheme
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: George is plotting something that involves one person tailing a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'George' looks like a man's name, but pilots have long nicknamed the autopilot George. 'Car' gives a whole word, the kind of car with self-changing gears.
explanation.definitionFit: George is long-standing aviation slang for the device that flies a plane without the human at the controls.

clue.text: Mass burial twice in awfully catastrophic year

definitions.note: ironic: literally a year of wonders, but the phrase is famously applied to 1666

indicators.note: something done awfully is done badly, leaving the letters in a mess to be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the little word in, written two times

explanation.surface: A mass grave dug in a terrible year of plague or war.
explanation.walkthrough: Latin for 'year of wonders'; Dryden's poem of that name covers 1666, the year of the Great Fire of London and plague, hence the ironic 'catastrophic'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dryden used the Latin phrase for 1666, a twelvemonth of plague, war and the Great Fire, so it labels a disastrous stretch of time here.

clue.text: Big cheese beat restriction, having discovered tax not applicable

indicators.note: dis-covered means with its covering taken away, so the outside letters go and the middle stays

blocks.note: to top is to beat or better
a ban is a restriction
the centre letter of tax
N/A is the standard form-filling abbreviation

explanation.surface: A boss overturned a restriction after finding a tax didn't apply to them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' reads as 'found out', but here it strips the covering letters from tax. N/A is what you write on a form for 'not applicable'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal phrases for the most important person in an organisation, the boss or leading figure.

clue.text: Mankini looked “lovely” on vacation - euphemistic to put it thus

definitions.note: the answer completes the phrase 'to put it ___', an adverb

indicators.note: a place on vacation is vacated, emptied of its contents, leaving only the outer letters

blocks.note: first and last letters
first and last letters
first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone in a mankini on holiday is politely described as looking 'lovely'.
explanation.walkthrough: The quote marks around 'lovely' hint at understatement: calling a mankini lovely is putting it gently. 'On vacation' sounds like a beach holiday but empties each word.
explanation.definitionFit: To put something mildly is to state it in a softened, understated way, which is what a euphemism does.

clue.text: Unusual result, ergo, put a pin in it

indicators.note: an unusual version departs from the normal order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An odd outcome, therefore shelve the matter for later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put a pin in it' is office jargon for postponing, but read literally it describes pinning a hem when taking up a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A tailor pins a hem in the lower part of a pair of slacks before sewing it, so that piece of clothing is literally where the pin goes.

clue.text: Ruminate about shape

blocks.note: c. is short for circa, about
to hew is to shape by cutting

explanation.surface: Thinking deeply about shape and form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like part of 'ruminate about', but it gives C, from circa.
explanation.definitionFit: To ruminate is literally to chew the cud, and figuratively to chew over an idea.

clue.text: See 1
Run off after writer - she waited a long time

blocks.note: a pen is a writing tool
to elope is to run off to marry

explanation.surface: A woman was left waiting for years after an author ran off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the running off behind the writer. 'Writer' is the implement, not an author.
explanation.definitionFit: In Homer's Odyssey, Odysseus's wife stayed faithful for twenty years while he was away at Troy and wandering home.

clue.text: Green field fairly empty

indicators.note: an empty word has had its insides removed, so only the outermost letters remain

blocks.note: a lea is a meadow, a poetic word for a field
first and last letters

explanation.surface: A green field that's pretty much deserted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fairly empty' reads as 'quite deserted', but 'fairly' is the word being emptied. LEA is a crossword staple for a meadow.
explanation.definitionFit: A leafy suburb or lane is full of trees and foliage, so the word describes somewhere verdant and green.

clue.text: Directories help one to be organised, fair and ultimately scrupulous

indicators.note: to organise is to put into a new arrangement, so the letters are reordered
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is wanted

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, also part of the mix
fair, in the sense of all right or acceptable
last letter

explanation.surface: Directories help a person be organised, fair and scrupulous in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To be' looks like grammar joining the phrase, but its letters are part of the mixture with 'help one'.
explanation.definitionFit: Printed listings of subscribers' names and numbers were the standard reference directories before the internet.

clue.text: Plane diverted somewhere in Asia

indicators.note: a diverted thing is sent off its usual course, so the letters take a new route

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A flight is diverted and lands somewhere in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a genuine travel scenario; the diversion happens to the letters of the aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: This Himalayan country lies between India and China, so it is a location on that continent.

clue.text: Sacking every good person, rock station put off everybody

indicators.note: to sack someone is to dismiss them, so letters are thrown out of each word

blocks.note: a stone is a rock
a stand, as in a taxi stand, is a station
to stall is to put off or delay
ST, saint, is the good person; 'every' means each word loses one

explanation.surface: A rock radio station sacks all its good staff and alienates everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock station' looks like one radio station, but rock, station and put off are three separate words, each losing its ST.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means every single person collectively, as in a greeting addressed to all present.

clue.text: Flowing waters engulf men with one going missing

indicators.note: something going missing disappears, so a letter is taken away
to engulf is to swallow up, so one piece ends up inside the other

blocks.note: seas are bodies of water
men are males
a, the indefinite article, means one

explanation.surface: Floodwaters sweep men away and one of them is lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flowing' sits next to 'waters' as if describing them, but it is the definition. 'One' is the article A, which is what goes missing from the men.
explanation.definitionFit: Smooth, continuous work or movement without visible joins or breaks is described as having no seams.

clue.text: Exaggerate malfunction

blocks.note: first meaning: to overstate or emphasise something
second meaning: of a machine, to misbehave or go wrong

explanation.walkthrough: Two separate senses of one phrasal verb; 'my knee is playing up' is the British use for a body part or machine failing.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb covers both emphasising a point beyond its worth and equipment misbehaving or failing to work properly.

clue.text: Failing to meet man right before death

indicators.note: something failing is breaking down, so the letters collapse and are rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone fails to meet a man just before he dies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right before death' reads as 'just before death', but 'right' supplies a letter and 'before death' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase literally means prior to dying, used in medicine and law for things done while still alive.

clue.text: Luvvie going over to embrace with smoochy sound

indicators.note: going over means turning over, flipping the word end to end
to embrace is to hug, holding something inside the arms

blocks.note: a luvvie is a gushing theatrical type; a ham is an overacting performer
W is the abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: A theatrical type comes over for a hug and an air kiss.
explanation.walkthrough: Luvvie is British slang for a showy, effusive actor, so HAM fits. 'To embrace' sounds like hugging but puts W inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The exaggerated air-kiss noise, written as an interjection, is the stereotypical greeting of theatrical people.

clue.text: See 1
Joanna (my Mum’s mum) paid for renovation? Over my dead body!

indicators.note: something up for renovation is going to be remade, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: your mother's mother is your gran
taken as written
the exclamation is an emphatic refusal

explanation.surface: Joanna's grandmother paid to have something restored, and someone flatly objects.
explanation.walkthrough: Joanna looks like a woman's name, but it is Cockney rhyming slang for a piano (Joanna rhymes with 'pianner').
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang turns the musical instrument into a girl's name; the large concert version is one example of that keyboard.

clue.text: Aisling Bea briefly floundering - way to let people down!

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the word loses its end
floundering is struggling clumsily, so the letters thrash about into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the name with its last letter cut

explanation.surface: The comedian Aisling Bea floundering on stage lets her audience down.
explanation.walkthrough: Aisling Bea is an Irish comedian and actor. 'Let people down' sounds like disappointing them, but it means lowering them literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Descending a cliff or wall on a fixed rope is a method of lowering climbers safely to the ground.

clue.text: Navvy’s dog more sullen when daughter's not around

indicators.note: something not around is absent, so that letter is dropped

blocks.note: a lab is a Labrador, a breed of dog
dour means sullen, so more sullen is dourer
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A workman's dog gets grumpier when his daughter isn't there.
explanation.walkthrough: A navvy is a British term for a manual worker on roads or railways. The 's means 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Navvies were the manual workers who dug Britain's canals and railways, so the word is a synonym for a manual worker.

clue.text: Struggling, naked, are we born again?

indicators.note: struggling suggests writhing and twisting, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Struggling and naked like newborns, have we been born again?
explanation.walkthrough: Naked struggling fits the image of birth; the question mark softens 'born again' as a figurative definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Being roused again into life or awareness is a figurative rebirth, the sense of a revived spirit.

clue.text: Rum, say, is licensed exclusively at first

indicators.note: at first points to the beginning, so only the opening letter of each word counts

blocks.note: taken as written
first letter
first letter

explanation.surface: Rum and similar drinks are sold only on licensed premises.
explanation.walkthrough: Rum looks like the drink, but it is a small island in Scotland's Inner Hebrides; 'say' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Rum is one of the Small Isles off Scotland's west coast, so it is an example of an island.

clue.text: State in North America welcoming drummer Grohl turning up

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means flipping a word to read from bottom to top
to welcome is to take in a guest, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation
Dave Grohl drummed for Nirvana before founding the Foo Fighters

explanation.surface: A US state welcomes Dave Grohl as he arrives for a gig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State in North America' reads as one long definition, but only 'State' defines; 'in' is a link and North America gives NA.
explanation.definitionFit: Nevada is one of the fifty United States, home to Las Vegas, so it is an example of a state.

clue.text: Announce sailor from the East’s election

indicators.note: in an across clue, east is the right-hand end, so reading from there runs backwards

blocks.note: a bell tolls to announce a death or an hour
AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor from the Orient is announced as the result of an election.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From the East' suggests the sailor's origin, but it applies to both pieces together, read right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballot is a vote, especially a secret one, and so stands for the process of choosing by voting.

clue.text: US bank oddly lied to recruit First Lady

indicators.note: oddly points to the odd-numbered positions, keeping every other letter from the start
to recruit is to bring someone into a group, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: first and third letters
Eve was the first woman in Genesis

explanation.surface: An American bank strangely lied in order to sign up the President's wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First Lady' suggests the US President's wife, but in crosswords it is usually Eve, the first woman.
explanation.definitionFit: On the Mississippi and other American rivers, an embankment built to prevent flooding has this name.

clue.text: Wing, maybe pro-British, inspiring return of imperial measurement

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the word runs backwards
to inspire is literally to breathe in, so one piece is drawn inside another

blocks.note: pro means in favour of
B is the abbreviation for British
the mile is a unit in the old imperial system

explanation.surface: A political wing, perhaps pro-British, inspires a return to imperial measures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wing' and 'pro-British' paint a political faction, but the wing is a bird's, and 'pro' and 'British' are two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird's wing evolved from the front pair of limbs, so it is one example of a front appendage.

clue.text: See 8
Very impressive bit of extreme picnicking

indicators.note: a bit of something is a small section, so the letters are a run lifted from inside the phrase

blocks.note: letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A spot of extreme picnicking sounds very impressive.
explanation.walkthrough: The run straddles the word break between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: In modern slang the word means outstanding or awesome, from its sense of grand heroic scale.

clue.text: Transcends right and wrong reversing sign of aging

indicators.note: to reverse is to go backwards, so the whole string reads from end to start

blocks.note: to top is to exceed or transcend
R is the abbreviation for right
evil is wrong, as in moral wrongdoing

explanation.surface: Something beyond right and wrong turns back the signs of age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right and wrong' reads as morality but splits into two pieces; the definition is the last three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Brown patches that appear on the skin of older people, especially the hands, are a common visible mark of getting old.

clue.text: Friend from Potsdam I googled

indicators.note: from means taken out of, so the letters are drawn straight out of the phrase

blocks.note: letters spanning three words

explanation.surface: Someone looked up a friend from the German city of Potsdam online.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is Spanish, though the surface sets it in Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish word for a pal is widely borrowed into English as a casual term for a companion.

clue.text: Political skullduggery as small business replaced MP’s car again

definitions.note: a mass noun defining a plural

indicators.note: read as re-placed: the letters are put into different positions

blocks.note: SME stands for small and medium-sized enterprise
taken as written
taken as written, also part of the mix

explanation.surface: Dirty politics as a small firm swaps out an MP's car once more.
explanation.walkthrough: SME is business jargon for a small or medium-sized enterprise. 'Replaced' signals the letters of the following words being placed anew.
explanation.definitionFit: Organised efforts to damage an opponent's reputation with rumour are a typical form of underhand political trickery.
